notes: 2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (ἀγαθός, ἀγαθή, ἀγαθόν): masc./neut. like λόγος and ἔργον, fem. like ἀρχή.
Oxytone: circumflex on the ending in the genitive and dative (ἀγαθοῦ, ἀγαθῇ, ἀγαθῶν, ἀγαθοῖς).
α-contract verb: α + ε > α, α + ο/ω > ω, α + ει/ῃ > ᾳ; infinitive ἀγαπᾶν.
The stem vowel lengthens to η before tense suffixes (ἀγαπήσω, ἠγάπησα, ἠγαπήθην).
First declension feminine in -η: ἀγάπη, ἀγάπης.
Plural ἀγάπαι “love feasts” (Jude 12).
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η; oxytone. Verbal adjective of ἀγαπάω “love”.
Vocative ἀγαπητοί “beloved” opens many exhortations; ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός “my beloved Son”.
Second declension masculine; accent moves to the penult before a long ending (ἀγγέλου, ἀγγέλων).
γγ is pronounced ng, as in English “angel”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ι (ἅγιος, ἁγία, ἅγιον).
Accent on the antepenult, moving to the penult before a long ending (ἁγίου, ἁγία, ἁγίων).
οἱ ἅγιοι “the saints”; τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον “the Holy Spirit”.
Reduplicated 2nd aorist ἤγαγον (stem ἀγαγ-); aorist passive ἤχθην.
Imperative ἄγε also means “come now!” (Jas 4:13; 5:1).
Second declension masculine; oxytone (ἀδελφοῦ, ἀδελφῷ). Vocative ἀδελφέ, plural ἀδελφοί.
The plural ἀδελφοί can include women: “brothers and sisters”, fellow believers.
Third declension neuter, stem αἱματ-: αἷμα, αἵματος.
Liquid verb: contract future ἀρῶ, aorist ἦρα (no σ); aorist infinitive ἆραι, imperative ἆρον.
Aorist passive ἤρθην.
ε-contract verb with augment αι > ῃ (ᾔτησα); middle αἰτοῦμαι is used with little difference in meaning.
Third declension, stem αἰων-: ν drops before σι (αἰῶσι); vocative = nominative.
εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα “forever”; εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων “forever and ever”.
Two endings in the NT: the masculine forms serve for the feminine too (ζωὴ αἰώνιος “eternal life”).
A three-ending feminine αἰωνίαν occurs twice (2 Thess 2:16; Heb 9:12).
ε-contract verb; takes a dative object (“follow someone”).
Object in the genitive (person or sound) or accusative (thing heard).
Future ἀκούσω and middle ἀκούσομαι (same meaning); perfect ἀκήκοα (Attic reduplication).
First declension feminine with short -α after ι: genitive ἀληθείας, dative ἀληθείᾳ (the long endings pull the accent to the penult).
ἐπ’ ἀληθείας “truly”.
Strong “but, rather”, especially after a negative: οὐ … ἀλλά “not … but”.
Elided ἀλλ’ before a vowel.
Reciprocal “one another”: plural only, with no nominative.
Formed from ἄλλος doubled (ἀλλ-ηλ-); ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους “love one another”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η, but neuter singular ἄλλο without -ν (like αὐτό, τοῦτο).
οἱ ἄλλοι “the others”; ἄλλοι … ἄλλοι “some … others”.
Nasal present; 2nd aorist ἥμαρτον, future ἁμαρτήσω, perfect ἡμάρτηκα.
The NT also has a 1st aorist ἡμάρτησα: ἁμαρτήσῃ, ἁμαρτήσωμεν, ἁμαρτήσας.
First declension feminine in -α (after ι): ἁμαρτία, ἁμαρτίας. Genitive plural ἁμαρτιῶν.
Two endings: ἁμαρτωλός (masc./fem.), ἁμαρτωλόν (neut.); oxytone, so circumflex in genitive and dative.
Often a noun: “a sinner”, οἱ ἁμαρτωλοί; ἁμαρτωλός of a woman in Luke 7:37.
Hebrew “surely, truly”: closes prayers and doxologies (“amen”).
Jesus’ ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν “truly I tell you” (doubled in John: ἀμὴν ἀμήν).
A particle of contingency, usually untranslated: after relatives and conjunctions with the subjunctive it gives “-ever” (ὃς ἄν “whoever”; ὅταν = ὅτε + ἄν).
With a past indicative in an unreal condition it means “would”.
Root aorist ἀνέβην (imperative ἀνάβηθι, inf. ἀναβῆναι, ptc. ἀναβάς); future middle ἀναβήσομαι with active meaning.
NT imperatives also ἀνάβα, ἀνάβατε (Koine).
Third declension i-stem like πόλις: ἀνάστασις, ἀναστάσεως.
From ἀνίστημι “raise, rise”: ἡ ἀνάστασις τῶν νεκρῶν “the resurrection of the dead”.
Third declension with stem ἀνδρ- (δ inserted between ν and ρ): ἀνδρός, ἄνδρα, ἀνδράσι(ν); vocative ἄνερ.
An adult male or a husband; ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί “brothers!” in speeches in Acts.
Second declension masculine; accent moves from the antepenult to the penult before a long ending (ἀνθρώπου, ἀνθρώπῳ, ἀνθρώπων).
Means a human being of either sex; ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου “the Son of Man”.
Compound of ἵστημι: 1st aorist ἀνέστησα “I raised” (transitive), 2nd aorist ἀνέστην “I rose” (intransitive).
Middle ἀνίσταμαι and future middle ἀναστήσομαι are intransitive “rise”; NT imperative also ἀνάστα (for ἀνάστηθι).
The augment varies and can be double: ἤνοιξα, ἀνέῳξα, ἠνέῳξα; perfect ἀνέῳγα, ἀνέῳγμαι (NT also ἠνεῳγμένος).
Aorist passive ἠνεῴχθην, ἀνεῴχθην, ἠνοίχθην or 2nd aorist ἠνοίγην; future passive ἀνοιγήσομαι.
Liquid verb: contract future ἀπαγγελῶ, aorist ἀπήγγειλα; 2nd aorist passive ἀπηγγέλην.
Compound of ἔρχομαι: aorist ἀπῆλθον, perfect ἀπελήλυθα; deponent (middle forms, active meaning) in present and future.
NT 1st-aorist endings: ἀπῆλθαν, ἀπῆλθα.
“from, away from” (separation, origin); also cause “because of”.
Elided ἀπ’, before a rough breathing ἀφ’ (ἀφ’ οὗ “since”).
Compound of δίδωμι: ἀπέδωκα, ἀπόδος, ἀποδοῦναι; aorist middle ἀπεδόμην “sold”.
NT variants: ἀπέδετο (Heb 12:16), imperfect ἀπεδίδουν, ptc. ἀποδιδοῦν.
Present with -ισκ- suffix and iota subscript; 2nd aorist ἀπέθανον.
Future ἀποθανοῦμαι is middle (contract) with active meaning; the perfect is supplied by τέθνηκα.
Deponent: the usual aorist is passive in form with active meaning, ἀπεκρίθην “I answered” (ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν “he answered and said”).
Liquid stem: the rarer aorist middle ἀπεκρινάμην (ἀπεκρίνατο, 7×) has no σ.
Liquid verb: contract future ἀποκτενῶ, aorist ἀπέκτεινα; aorist passive ἀπεκτάνθην.
NT also has the present stem ἀποκτέννω (ἀποκτέννει, ἀποκτέννοντες).
-νυμι type μι-verb. Active “destroy, lose”: ἀπολέσω, ἀπώλεσα; middle “perish”: ἀπόλλυμαι, ἀπολοῦμαι, 2nd aorist ἀπωλόμην.
2nd perfect ἀπόλωλα “I am lost” (intransitive).
NT variants with thematic endings: ἀπολλύει, ἀπόλλυε; future also ἀπολῶ (1 Cor 1:19).
Compound of λύω, conjugated like it; augment after the prefix (ἀπέλυσα, ἀπελύθην).
Liquid verb: contract future ἀποστελῶ, aorist ἀπέστειλα (ε > ει, no σ).
Stem σταλ- in perfect and 2nd aorist passive (ἀπέσταλκα, ἀπέσταλμαι, ἀπεστάλην); NT perfect 3 pl also ἀπέσταλκαν.
Second declension masculine; accent moves to the penult before a long ending (ἀποστόλου, ἀποστόλων).
From ἀποστέλλω “send out”: one sent, a messenger.
Inferential “so, then, consequently”; ἄρα οὖν “so then” (Paul).
Distinguish the interrogative particle ἆρα (with circumflex).
Second declension masculine, like λόγος.
A loaf; “bread” in general; ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως “bread of the Presence”.
First declension feminine in -η; oxytone (ἀρχῆς, ἀρχῇ).
ἐν ἀρχῇ “in the beginning”; plural ἀρχαί “rulers, powers”.
Third declension in -ευς like βασιλεύς: ἀρχιερεύς, ἀρχιερέως.
ἀρχ- “chief” + ἱερεύς “priest”; plural οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς “the chief priests”.
Active “rule” (with genitive) is rare; the common NT use is middle ἄρχομαι “begin”, usually with an infinitive.
Aorist middle ἠρξάμην, future middle ἄρξομαι.
Deponent -άζομαι verb (middle forms, active meaning): aorist ἠσπασάμην; imperative ἀσπάσασθε “greet” in letters.
Declined like ἀγαθός, but the neuter singular is αὐτό (no -ν).
Three uses: “he, she, it, they” (mostly in the oblique cases); intensive “-self” (αὐτὸς ὁ …); “same” after the article (ὁ αὐτός).
Compound of ἵημι: κ-aorist ἀφῆκα in the indicative, root ἑ- elsewhere (ἀφῶ, ἄφες, ἀφεῖναι, ἀφείς).
Koine perfect passive ἀφέωνται (Attic ἀφεῖνται); imperfect ἤφιεν with the augment on the prefix.
NT variants with thematic endings: ἀφεῖς, ἀφίομεν, ἀφίουσι(ν); aorist 2 sg ἀφῆκες.
“until, as far as”; ἄχρι οὗ “until”.
Also spelled ἄχρις before a vowel.
Liquid verb: contract future βαλῶ, 2nd aorist ἔβαλον (NT also ἔβαλαν).
Stem βλη- in perfect and aorist passive (βέβληκα, βέβλημαι, ἐβλήθην).
-ίζω verb: ζ becomes σ before σ/θ (βαπτίσω, ἐβαπτίσθην); middle βαπτίσαι “have yourself baptized” (Acts 22:16).
First declension feminine in -α (after ι): βασιλεία, βασιλείας. Genitive plural βασιλειῶν.
Nominative plural βασιλεῖαι: circumflex because the final -αι counts as short.
Third declension in -ευς: βασιλεύς, βασιλέως, βασιλεῖ, βασιλέα; plural βασιλεῖς, βασιλέων.
Accusative plural βασιλεῖς in the NT (Attic βασιλέας). Vocative βασιλεῦ.
Labial stem: π + σ > ψ (βλέψω, ἔβλεψα); the NT uses mostly the present.
Postpositive: gives the reason or explanation — “for”.
First declension feminine in -α (after ε); oxytone, so circumflex in the genitive and dative (γενεᾶς, γενεᾷ).
α-contract verb; “beget, father” (of the father) or “bear” (of the mother); passive “be born”.
Contracted first declension (from γέα): circumflex throughout (γῆ, γῆς, γῇ, γῆν).
No plural in the NT.
Deponent: middle forms with active meaning; 2nd aorist middle ἐγενόμην (μὴ γένοιτο “may it not be”), also passive-form ἐγενήθην.
Perfect γέγονα is active in form; the pluperfect appears with and without augment (ἐγεγόνει, γεγόνει).
NT perfect 3 pl also γέγοναν.
Present with -σκ- suffix (Attic γιγνώσκω); future middle γνώσομαι with active meaning.
Root aorist ἔγνων: subj. γνῶ, imperative γνῶθι, inf. γνῶναι, ptc. γνούς.
NT variants: subjunctive γνοῖ (for γνῷ), perfect 3 pl ἔγνωκαν.
First declension feminine with short -α after σσ: genitive γλώσσης.
The circumflex becomes acute before a long ending (γλώσσης, γλώσσαις).
Third declension in -ευς like βασιλεύς: γραμματεύς, γραμματέως.
From γράμμα “letter, writing”: an expert in the Law.
First declension feminine in -η; oxytone (γραφῆς, γραφῇ).
αἱ γραφαί “the Scriptures”.
Labial stem: φ + σ > ψ (γράψω, ἔγραψα); perfect passive γέγραπται “it is written”.
2nd aorist passive ἐγράφη (no θ); perfect middle/passive 3 pl is periphrastic (γεγραμμένοι εἰσί).
Irregular: nominative γυνή, every other form from the third-declension stem γυναικ-; vocative γύναι.
Genitive and dative accent the ending (γυναικός, γυναικί, γυναικῶν); dative plural γυναιξί(ν).
Second declension neuter; accent moves to the penult before a long ending (δαιμονίου).
Postpositive (never first in its clause): “but, and, now”, marking a new step or a mild contrast.
μέν … δέ “on the one hand … on the other”; ὁ δέ “and he”. Elided δ’ before a vowel.
Impersonal (3 sg only), usually with accusative + infinitive: δεῖ με ἐλθεῖν “I must come”.
Imperfect ἔδει “it was necessary”; ptc. τὸ δέον “what is needed”, τὰ μὴ δέοντα (1 Tim 5:13).
MorphGNT files these forms under δέω; they are counted here.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ι (δεξιός, δεξιά, δεξιόν); oxytone.
ἡ δεξιά (supply χείρ) “the right hand”; ἐκ δεξιῶν “at the right”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ρ (δεύτερος, δευτέρα, δεύτερον).
Ordinal “second”; ἐκ δευτέρου “a second time”.
Deponent (middle forms, active meaning); guttural stem: aorist ἐδεξάμην, perfect δέδεγμαι.
Contract verb with monosyllabic stem: aorist ἔδησα, perfect passive δέδεμαι, aorist passive ἐδέθην.
MorphGNT also files δεῖ (listed separately) and ten forms of δέομαι “ask” (ἐδεήθην, δεήθητε, δεόμενος) under δέω; they are not shown here.
NT count excludes the 10 forms of δέομαι “ask” that MorphGNT files under δέω.
+ gen. “through, by means of”; + acc. “because of, on account of”.
διὰ τοῦτο “therefore”; διὰ τί “why?”. Elided δι’ before a vowel.
Second declension masculine; accent moves to the penult before a long ending (διδασκάλου). Vocative διδάσκαλε “Teacher!”.
-σκ- present; stem διδαχ-: διδάξω, ἐδίδαξα, ἐδιδάχθην.
μι-verb with reduplicated present stem διδο-; long stem δω- in future and aorist (δώσω, ἔδωκα).
κ-aorist ἔδωκα in the indicative; other moods use the short root δο-: δῶ, δός, δοῦναι, δούς.
NT variants: subjunctive δοῖ, δώῃ, δώσῃ (for δῷ); optative δῴη (for δοίη); imperfect 3 pl ἐδίδουν.
Compound of ἔρχομαι: aorist διῆλθον, perfect διελήλυθα; deponent (middle forms, active meaning) in present, imperfect and future.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ι (δίκαιος, δικαία, δίκαιον).
Accent moves to the penult before a long ending (δικαίου, δικαία); final -αι, -οι count as short (δίκαιαι, δίκαιοι).
First declension feminine in -η: δικαιοσύνη, δικαιοσύνης.
διά + ὅ: “therefore, for this reason”.
Guttural stem: διώξω, ἐδίωξα, ἐδιώχθην, perfect passive δεδίωγμαι.
ε-contract in the present, but aorist ἔδοξα (stem δοκ- + σ); impersonal δοκεῖ μοι “it seems to me”.
First declension feminine with short -α (not after ε, ι, ρ): genitive δόξης, dative δόξῃ.
-άζω verb: ζ becomes σ (δοξάσω, ἐδόξασα, ἐδοξάσθην); perfect passive δεδόξασμαι.
Second declension masculine; circumflex becomes acute before a long ending (δούλου, δούλων). Vocative δοῦλε.
Also an adjective “enslaved”: neuter plural δοῦλα (Rom 6:19, twice).
Deponent μι-type verb (stem δυνα-): δύναμαι, δύνασαι, δύναται; NT 2 sg also δύνῃ.
Augment ἐ- or ἠ- (ἐδύνατο, ἠδύνατο); the aorist is passive in form, ἠδυνήθην “I was able”.
Third declension i-stem like πόλις: δύναμις, δυνάμεως, δυνάμει, δύναμιν.
Plural δυνάμεις “miracles, mighty works”; also “powers” (spiritual beings).
Indeclinable except the dative δυσί(ν); same form for all genders (Attic genitive/dative δυοῖν).
οἱ δύο “the two”; ἀνὰ δύο “two by two”.
Indeclinable numeral (δύο + δέκα “two + ten”).
οἱ δώδεκα “the Twelve” (disciples).
εἰ + ἄν: “if” with the subjunctive, for a condition that may or may not be met.
After a relative it can stand for ἄν: ὃς ἐάν “whoever”.
Reflexive: no nominative; it points back to the subject (“himself, herself, itself”).
The plural also serves the first and second persons: “ourselves, yourselves, themselves”.
Contracted αὑτοῦ, αὑτῷ, αὑτόν … (rough breathing!) also occur; do not confuse with αὐτοῦ.
-ίζω verb; Attic-type contract future ἐγγιῶ (ἐγγιεῖ, Jas 4:8); perfect ἤγγικεν “has come near”.
Liquid verb: contract future ἐγερῶ, aorist ἤγειρα without σ; perfect passive ἐγήγερμαι (Attic reduplication).
Aorist passive ἠγέρθην often means “rose” (intransitive).

ego.mean: I, me; pl. ἡμεῖς we, us
notes: MorphGNT files the plural ἡμεῖς under ἐγώ, so both numbers are shown.
μου, μοι, με are enclitic; the emphatic ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ are used for contrast and after most prepositions.
The nominative ἐγώ is emphatic: the verb ending already shows “I”.
Third declension neuter, stem ἐθνεσ-: σ drops between vowels and the vowels contract (ἔθνους, plural ἔθνη, ἐθνῶν).
τὰ ἔθνη “the nations, the Gentiles”.
“if”, usually with the indicative (rarely the optative); “whether” in indirect questions.
εἰ μή “except, unless”; εἰ καί “even if”. A proclitic.
Irregular μι-verb; the present indicative forms except εἶ are enclitic.
Imperfect 1 sg ἤμην and 1 pl ἤμεθα are Koine middle-type endings (Attic ἦ/ἦν, ἦμεν); 2 sg also ἦσθα.
Future ἔσομαι is middle in form (3 sg ἔσται); NT imperative 3 sg also ἤτω (1 Cor 16:22, Jas 5:12).
First declension feminine in -η: εἰρήνη, εἰρήνης.
Echoes Hebrew šālôm; a common greeting.
Motion “into, to”; goal or purpose “for” (εἰς τό + infinitive “in order to”); also “against”.
A proclitic. Do not confuse εἰς “into” with εἷς “one”.
Masculine and neuter third declension (stem ἑν-: ἑνός, ἑνί), feminine first declension (μία, μιᾶς, μιᾷ); singular only.
Distinguish εἷς “one” from the preposition εἰς and ἕν “one (neut.)” from ἐν “in”.
Can mean “a certain” or “first”: μία τῶν σαββάτων “the first day of the week”.
Compound of ἔρχομαι: aorist εἰσῆλθον, perfect εἰσελήλυθα; deponent (middle forms, active meaning) in present and future.
NT 1st-aorist endings: εἰσήλθατε, εἰσέλθατε, εἰσελθάτω.
εἰ + τε: εἴτε … εἴτε “whether … or”.
“out of, from” (source, origin, separation); also “by means of, because of”.
Before a vowel it becomes ἐξ (ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ἐξ ὕψους).
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (ἕκαστος, ἑκάστη, ἕκαστον); almost always singular.
Often with a partitive genitive: ἕκαστος ὑμῶν “each of you”.
Compound of βάλλω (ἐκ > ἐξ before the augment): ἐξέβαλον, ἐκβαλῶ, ἐξεβλήθην.
“there”; ἐκεῖθεν “from there”. Related to ἐκεῖνος “that”.
Declined like αὐτός (neuter ἐκεῖνο without -ν); circumflex becomes acute before a long ending (ἐκείνου).
“That” (more remote than οὗτος), in predicate position: ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις “in those days”; alone often “he” (John).
First declension feminine in -α (after ι): ἐκκλησία, ἐκκλησίας.
Originally a citizens’ assembly; in the NT the church, local or universal.
Third declension, stem ἐλπιδ-: δ drops before σ (ἐλπίς, ἐλπίσι); vocative ἐλπί.
ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι “in hope”.
Possessive adjective of ἐγώ, declined like ἀγαθός (ἐμός, ἐμή, ἐμόν); more emphatic than μου.
The other possessives work the same way: σός “your (sg.)”, ἡμέτερος “our”, ὑμέτερος “your (pl.)”.
“in front of, before” (place, also “in the sight of”); as an adverb “ahead”.
Place “in, among”; time “in, during”; means “by, with” (ἐν μαχαίρῃ “with a sword”).
ἐν τῷ + infinitive “while, when”. A proclitic: it has no accent of its own.
First declension feminine in -η; oxytone (ἐντολῆς, ἐντολῇ).
“before, in the presence of, in the sight of”; frequent in Luke, Acts and Revelation.
An “improper” preposition: originally an adverb and never a verb prefix.
Compound of ἔρχομαι (ἐκ > ἐξ): aorist ἐξῆλθον, perfect ἐξελήλυθα; deponent (middle forms, active meaning) in present, imperfect and future.
NT 1st-aorist endings: ἐξήλθατε, ἐξῆλθαν, ἐξέλθατε.
First declension feminine in -α (after ι): ἐξουσία, ἐξουσίας.
Adverb “outside, out” (ἐξῆλθεν ἔξω “he went out”); as an improper preposition + gen. “outside of”.
οἱ ἔξω “outsiders”.
First declension feminine in -α (after ι): ἐπαγγελία, ἐπαγγελίας.
α-contract compound of ἐρωτάω; augment after the prefix: ἐπηρώτων, ἐπηρώτησα.
+ gen. “on, upon; before; in the time of”; + dat. “on, at; on the basis of”; + acc. “on, onto, to, against, over”.
Elided ἐπ’ before a smooth breathing, ἐφ’ before a rough breathing (ἐφ’ ᾧ).
Compound of γινώσκω: root aorist ἐπέγνων, future middle ἐπιγνώσομαι (active meaning), aorist passive ἐπεγνώσθην.
Indeclinable numeral: the same form for every case and gender.
Prominent in Revelation (seven churches, seals, trumpets, bowls).
Second declension neuter: nominative = accusative; plural ἔργα.
A neuter plural subject often takes a singular verb.
Two endings: ἔρημος (masc./fem.), ἔρημον (neut.).
ἡ ἔρημος (supply γῆ or χώρα) is “the wilderness, desert”; ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ “in the wilderness”.
Deponent in the present, imperfect and future ἐλεύσομαι (middle forms, active meaning); suppletive aorist ἦλθον and perfect ἐλήλυθα are active.
2nd aorist imperative ἐλθέ is oxytone; NT also has 1st-aorist endings: ἦλθαν, ἤλθαμεν, ἤλθατε, ἐλθάτω.
α-contract verb; NT imperfect 3 pl also ἠρώτουν (ε-contract form).
Suppletive: aorist ἔφαγον, future φάγομαι (middle in form, no σ, active meaning).
NT variants: future 2 sg φάγεσαι (Luke 17:8), subjunctive ἔσθητε (Luke 22:30, from ἔσθω).
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (ἔσχατος, ἐσχάτη, ἔσχατον); accent moves to the penult before a long ending.
ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις “in the last days”; οἱ ἔσχατοι “the last”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ρ (ἕτερος, ἑτέρα, ἕτερον).
Often “another, a different one”, beside ἄλλος “another (of the same kind)”, though the NT does not always keep them apart.
“still, yet; further, more”; οὐκ … ἔτι “no longer”.
Third declension neuter like ἔθνος: ἔτος, ἔτους, plural ἔτη, ἐτῶν.
Mostly middle εὐαγγελίζομαι “proclaim the good news”; the active occurs only in Rev 10:7 and 14:6.
Augment after εὐ-: εὐηγγελιζόμην, εὐηγγελισάμην.
Second declension neuter; accent moves to the penult before a long ending (εὐαγγελίου).
εὐ- “good” + ἀγγελ- “message”.
Third/first declension adjective in -υς, -εια, -υ (like βαρύς, ὀξύς): stem εὐθε- in most masc./neut. forms, fem. εὐθεῖα, εὐθείας.

-ισκ- present; 2nd aorist εὗρον (imperative εὑρέ); aorist passive εὑρέθην usually without augment.

First declension feminine with short -α after σσ: genitive θαλάσσης, dative θαλάσσῃ.
Used also of the Sea of Galilee.

-άζω verb: ἐθαύμασα; the aorist passive ἐθαυμάσθην also means “marveled”.
Third declension neuter, stem θεληματ-: θέλημα, θελήματος.
From θέλω “want, will”.

Tenses other than the present add -η- (θελήσω, ἠθέλησα).

ε-contract verb, mostly present and imperfect in the NT (“watch, observe”).
Second declension neuter, like ἔργον. In Revelation τὸ θηρίον “the beast”.
Third declension i-stem like πόλις: θλῖψις, θλίψεως.
Long ι: circumflex θλῖψις, θλῖψιν; acute before a long ending (θλίψεως).
Second declension masculine, like λόγος.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ι (ἴδιος, ἰδία, ἴδιον); accent moves to the penult before a long ending.
κατ’ ἰδίαν “privately”; οἱ ἴδιοι “his own people”.
“Look! See! Behold!” — calls attention to what follows; καὶ ἰδού “and behold”.
Originally ἰδοῦ, the aorist middle imperative of εἶδον “see”, with the accent shifted.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ρ (ἱερός, ἱερά, ἱερόν).
In the NT almost always the neuter noun τὸ ἱερόν “the temple (precinct)”; τὰ ἱερά “sacred things”.
Second declension neuter; accent moves to the penult before a long ending (ἱματίου).
Plural τὰ ἱμάτια “clothes”.

hina.mean: so that, in order that; that
notes: Purpose “in order that, so that”, with the subjunctive.
Also “that” after verbs of asking, commanding, wishing (a Koine development).
μι-verb with reduplicated present (ἱ- < σι-). Two aorists: 1st ἔστησα “I set” (transitive), 2nd ἔστην “I stood” (intransitive).
Perfect ἕστηκα “I stand” and pluperfect εἱστήκειν “I was standing” have present/imperfect meaning; short forms ἑστάναι, ἑστώς.
NT also ἱστάνομεν (Rom 3:31, from ἱστάνω) and imperfect ἔστηκεν (John 8:44, from στήκω).

kago.mean: and I, I too, even I
notes: Crasis: καί and ἐγώ merge into one word; the coronis (’) over α marks the join.
“and I”, “I also”, “even I”. Only κἀγώ, κἀμοί, κἀμέ occur in the NT; κἀμοῦ is classical.
Deponent (middle forms, active meaning) with a perfect-like present: “I am seated”; it has no aorist (καθίζω supplies it).
Koine imperative κάθου (Attic κάθησο); NT 2 sg also κάθῃ.
Transitive “seat” or intransitive “sit down”; the augment stands before the prefix (ἐκάθισα).
“just as, as”; sometimes “since” or “how”. καθὼς γέγραπται “as it is written”.
Coordinating “and”; adverbial “also, even”.
καὶ … καί “both … and”.
Merges with a following word by crasis: κἀγώ, κἀκεῖ, κἄν.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (καινός, καινή, καινόν); oxytone.
ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη “the new covenant”; καινὴ κτίσις “new creation”.
Second declension masculine; oxytone (καιροῦ, καιρῷ).
A fixed or right time, a season, as against χρόνος, time as duration.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (κακός, κακή, κακόν); oxytone.
Often the neuter as a noun: τὸ κακόν, τὰ κακά “evil, harm”.
ε-contract verb that keeps ε short in the future and aorist (καλέσω, ἐκάλεσα).
Shortened stem κλη- in the perfect and aorist passive (κέκληκα, κέκλημαι, ἐκλήθην).
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (καλός, καλή, καλόν); oxytone.
“Good” in the sense of fine, noble, beautiful: ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός “the good shepherd”.
First declension feminine in -α (after ι): καρδία, καρδίας.
Second declension masculine; oxytone (καρποῦ, καρπῷ).
+ gen. “down from; against; throughout”; + acc. “according to, in accordance with; during; throughout”.
Distributive: καθ’ ἡμέραν “daily”, κατὰ πόλιν “city by city”. Elided κατ’, καθ’.
Root aorist κατέβην (imperative κατάβηθι, ptc. καταβάς); future middle καταβήσομαι with active meaning.
NT imperative 3 sg καταβάτω (for καταβήτω).
ε-contract compound; augment after the prefix: κατῴκησα.
First declension feminine in -η; oxytone (κεφαλῆς, κεφαλῇ).
-σσω verb with guttural stem κηρυκ-: κηρύξω, ἐκήρυξα, ἐκηρύχθην.
Second declension masculine, like λόγος.
Basic sense “order, adornment”; in John often the world of humanity.
Aorist ἔκραξα; 2nd perfect κέκραγα with present meaning (“cries out”).
NT also has the reduplicated aorist ἐκέκραξα (Acts 24:21).
ε-contract verb; with genitive “take hold of”, with accusative “seize, hold fast”; perfect passive κεκράτηνται (John 20:23).
Liquid verb: contract future κρινῶ, aorist ἔκρινα without σ.
Stem κρι- in the perfect and aorist passive (κέκρικα, κέκριμαι, ἐκρίθην).
Third declension i-stem like πόλις: κρίσις, κρίσεως.
ἡμέρα κρίσεως “day of judgment”.
Second declension masculine; the accent moves to the penult before a long ending (κυρίου, κυρίων).
Vocative κύριε “Lord!” or simply “sir”. ὁ κύριος renders the divine name in the Greek Old Testament.
ε-contract verb, regular throughout: λαλήσω, ἐλάλησα, λελάληκα, ἐλαλήθην.
Nasal-infix present (λα-μ-β-άν-ω); 2nd aorist ἔλαβον, perfect εἴληφα.
Future λήμψομαι is middle in form with active meaning; Koine spelling with μ (Attic λήψομαι).
Imperative λαβέ (Attic accent); the NT has λάβε.
Second declension masculine; oxytone (λαοῦ, λαῷ).
Often “the people” of Israel or of God.

Future ἐρῶ is contracted like a liquid future (ἐρεῖς, ἐρεῖ); NT perfect 3 pl also εἴρηκαν.
Second declension masculine, like λόγος.

ὁ λόγος “the Word” (John 1:1); also “account, matter, reason”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (λοιπός, λοιπή, λοιπόν); oxytone.

The model regular verb: λύσω, ἔλυσα, λέλυκα, λέλυμαι, ἐλύθην (υ long in present, future and aorist active, short elsewhere).
First declension masculine in -ης: genitive μαθητοῦ (-ου like the second declension), vocative μαθητά.
Oxytone, so circumflex in the genitive and dative (μαθητοῦ, μαθητῇ).
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ι (μακάριος, μακαρία, μακάριον).
Begins each Beatitude: μακάριοι οἱ … “blessed are those …”.
Comparative of the adverb μάλα “very”: “more, rather”.
μᾶλλον ἤ “rather than”; πολλῷ μᾶλλον “much more”.
ε-contract verb, regular (μαρτυρήσω, ἐμαρτύρησα, μεμαρτύρηκα); passive “be well spoken of”.

φωνῇ μεγάλῃ “with a loud voice”.
Usually with an infinitive: “be about to, intend”; ptc. τὸ μέλλον “the future”.
Augment ἠ- or ἐ- (ἤμελλον, ἔμελλον); future μελλήσω.

μὲν οὖν “so then”; οἱ μέν … οἱ δέ “some … others”.

2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (μέσος, μέση, μέσον).

μικρόν (neuter) “a little while”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (μόνος, μόνη, μόνον).

Second declension masculine; oxytone (ναοῦ, ναῷ).

2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ρ (νεκρός, νεκρά, νεκρόν); oxytone.
ἐκ νεκρῶν “from the dead”; οἱ νεκροί “the dead”.

ὁ νόμος often means the Law of Moses.
“now”; ὁ νῦν αἰών “the present age”; τὰ νῦν “now, as things are”.

One-syllable stem: νυκτός, νυκτί, νυκτῶν. νυκτός “by night” (genitive of time).

Oxytone (ὁδοῦ, ὁδῷ). In Acts ἡ ὁδός “the Way” names the Christian movement.
Perfect in form, present in meaning (“I know”); the pluperfect ᾔδειν is its past tense (“I knew”).
Stem varies οἰδ-/εἰδ-/ἰδ-: subj. εἰδῶ, inf. εἰδέναι, ptc. εἰδώς, imperative ἴσθι. MorphGNT files 24 forms of εἰδώς under ὁράω; they are shown here.
Koine plural οἴδαμεν, οἴδατε, οἴδασι(ν); the Attic forms ἴστε, ἴσασι(ν) also occur. Future εἰδήσω only in Heb 8:11.
First declension feminine in -α (after ι): οἰκία, οἰκίας.
Close in meaning to οἶκος.
Second declension masculine; circumflex becomes acute before a long ending (οἴκου, οἴκων).
Also “household, family”; κατ’ οἶκον “at home, from house to house”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -η (ὅλος, ὅλη, ὅλον).
Stands in predicate position: ὅλη ἡ πόλις “the whole city”; ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας “with all the heart”.
2-1-2 adjective with feminine in -α after ι (ὅμοιος, ὁμοία, ὅμοιον); the accent moves before a long ending.
Takes the dative: ὁμοία ἐστὶν … κόκκῳ σινάπεως “it is like a mustard seed”.
Third declension neuter, stem ὀνοματ-: ὄνομα, ὀνόματος, plural ὀνόματα.
The accent moves right as the word grows (ὀνόματος, ὀνομάτων). ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι “in the name”.
“where”; ὅπου ἄν / ὅπου ἐάν “wherever”.
Purpose “so that, in order that”, with the subjunctive; also “how” in indirect questions.
Suppletive: future ὄψομαι (middle, active meaning), aorist εἶδον (stem ἰδ-), perfect ἑώρακα, aorist passive ὤφθην “appeared”.
α-contract in the present (ὁρῶ, ὁρᾷς); imperative ἰδέ is oxytone in Attic, the NT has ἴδε.

Third declension neuter like ἔθνος: ὄρος, ὄρους, plural ὄρη.
Genitive plural in the NT is uncontracted ὀρέων (Rev 6:15) instead of Attic ὀρῶν.
Agrees with its antecedent in gender and number; its case comes from its role in its own clause (though it is often attracted to the antecedent’s case).
Always accented, unlike the article: ὅ “which” vs ὁ “the”, ἥ vs ἡ, οἵ vs οἱ, αἵ vs αἱ.
ἀφ’ οὗ “since”, ἕως οὗ “until”, ἀνθ’ ὧν “because”.

Often just “who”, sometimes “whoever” or “such as, the kind who”.
ὅτε + ἄν: “whenever, when”, usually with the subjunctive.
“when”, with the indicative, for a definite time.
“that” after verbs of saying, knowing, believing; “because” giving a reason.

οὐκ before a smooth breathing, οὐχ before a rough breathing (οὐκ ἔστιν, οὐχ ὁ).

Interjection “woe! alas!”, usually with the dative: οὐαὶ ὑμῖν “woe to you”.
οὐ + δέ: “and not, nor; not even”.
οὐδέ … οὐδέ “neither … nor”. Elided οὐδ’.
οὐδέ + εἷς, declined like εἷς (οὐδείς, οὐδεμία, οὐδέν); singular only.
The Hellenistic spelling with θ also occurs: οὐθέν, οὐθενός.
Neuter οὐδέν “nothing”, also adverbial “not at all”.
οὐκ + ἔτι: “no longer, no more”.
Postpositive: “so, therefore”; in John often a mere connective “then, so”.
Second declension masculine; oxytone (οὐρανοῦ, οὐρανῷ).
Often plural for “heaven”: ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν “the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew).
οὐ + τε: “and not”; οὔτε … οὔτε “neither … nor”.

In predicate position it means “this”: οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος / ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος; alone “he, this one”. διὰ τοῦτο “therefore”.
“so, thus, in this way”; οὕτως also “so much” (οὕτως ἠγάπησεν John 3:16).
οὕτως is the usual form; οὕτω (without ς) appears 4 times before a consonant.
Strengthened οὐ: “not, no”.
In questions it expects “yes”: οὐχὶ οὗτός ἐστιν …; “is this not …?”.
Second declension masculine; oxytone (ὀφθαλμοῦ, ὀφθαλμῷ).
Second declension masculine, like λόγος.
Plural ὄχλοι “crowds”.
Second declension neuter; diminutive of παῖς. Vocative παιδίον, plural παιδία “children!”.
“again”; also “back” and, in arguments, “on the other hand”.
+ gen. “from (the side of)”; + dat. “beside, with, in the sight of”; + acc. “beside, along; rather than, contrary to”.
Elided παρ’ before a vowel.
First declension feminine in -η; oxytone (παραβολῆς, παραβολῇ).

2nd aorist ἔπαθον (stem παθ-), 2nd perfect πέπονθα.

Vocative πάτερ “Father!”; ὁ πατήρ is also used in address.
Dental stem: πείσω, ἔπεισα, ἐπείσθην; middle/passive “obey, be persuaded”.
2nd perfect πέποιθα “I trust, am confident” (pluperfect ἐπεποίθει).
Labial stem: πέμψω, ἔπεμψα, ἐπέμφθην.
